title: MoBE: Mixture-of-Basis-Experts
one_liner: MoBE compresses giant expert networks by splitting each expert's weight matrix into a shared blueprint plus a small expert-specific tweak.
lead: Large language models with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture are fast because they only use a few of their thousands of experts at a time. But they still need enormous memory to store all those experts. MoBE shrinks them by discovering that many experts are similar — they can share a common core structure and only differ in small expert-specific parts.

paras: Large language models using Mixture-of-Experts store thousands of separate neural networks called experts. Each one is ready to run, so the model can pick a few fast experts for each question because the router (a small network that picks) only activates a few, and skipping the rest saves time. This makes inference (when the finished model answers a new question) quick, but the storage is massive because all those experts must be kept in memory even if only a few run, so a 671-billion-parameter (a parameter is a single number that the model learned) model needs enormous memory cards.

You might try just removing experts you do not use (expert pruning). This shrinks the model but breaks it: the model loses specialized knowledge and its answers get wrong on 7-14% of cases. You might try squashing expert matrices using compression techniques like SVD (a standard mathematical trick). Still too crude: even small compressions lose significant information because you treat each expert independently.
The hidden problem: experts are not randomly different. They are similar to each other within a layer. That similarity is going to waste.

callout.html: MoBE splits each expert weight matrix (a grid of learned numbers used in computation) as W equals A times B, where A is unique per expert but B is a shared blueprint matrix reused across all experts in that layer.

steps.text: Take each expert's weight matrix W from the pretrained model (e.g., Qwen3-235B).

steps.b: Decompose into W equals A times B
steps.text: Factor W as a product: A (small, expert-specific) times B (medium, layer-shared).

steps.b: Share the blueprint B across experts
steps.text: Instead of storing 10 separate B matrices, all experts in the layer use the same B.

steps.b: Tune A to minimize reconstruction loss
steps.text: Adjust each expert's A matrix so A times B still reconstructs W accurately.
Store one B per layer plus all A matrices; model size shrinks 24-30%.

paras: MoBE changes how expert weight matrices are stored and computed. Instead of keeping each expert's full matrix W, it splits W into two parts: a small expert-specific matrix A and a shared layer-wide blueprint matrix B. At inference time, the model still computes the same result by multiplying A times B, but the total storage is much smaller because B is reused across all experts.

The key is that A is unique per expert but B is identical across all experts within a single MoE layer. This asymmetry is what creates the compression: you save storage on B because you store it only once.

hidden.h2: Reconstruction Error: How Well the Decomposition Fits
hidden.name: mean squared error of factorization
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity: reconstruction error, the difference between the original weight matrix W and the reconstructed matrix A times B. This error is measured across all experts in a layer using mean squared error (MSE), which is just the average of all squared differences. Lower MSE means the factorization captures more of the original pattern.

MoBE estimates this by training the A and B matrices to minimize reconstruction error during the compression step. The paper shows (in their graphs) that MoBE achieves lower MSE than competing methods like MoLAE and D-squared-MoE across many layers of real models, which means more information is preserved even at high compression rates.

heat.caption: Darker means higher reconstruction error; marked cells show where basis factorization achieves especially good fit.

reads.html: Think of reconstruction error as how much information you lose when you fold a big poster into a small tube and then unfold it again. If the ink smudges a lot, error is high. MoBE finds a folding pattern that preserves as much as possible.

In Section 3.2, the paper minimizes the reconstruction error between the original weight matrices and the factorized representation W equals A times B using gradient descent (a method that adjusts all the numbers step by step to shrink the error), typically with the Adam optimizer. Figure 2-4 show per-layer MSE loss comparing MoBE to MoLAE and D-squared-MoE.

mechanism.h2: Why Shared Basis Compression Preserves Accuracy
paras: The core mechanism is that experts within a layer are structured: they have a common backbone plus expert-specific adjustments. By factorizing W equals A times B and sharing B across experts, MoBE exploits that structure. The shared matrix B encodes the backbone (what all experts do in common), and the expert-specific matrix A encodes the specialist knowledge (how each expert differs).

This works because the factorization respects the actual computation: at inference, the model still computes output equals input times A times B, which is mathematically identical to input times W when A times B equals W. So there is no approximation in the forward pass—only in how storage is organized. The only information loss comes from tuning A and B to approximately reconstruct W, but because B is large (shared across many experts) and A is small (only adjusts for one expert), the tuning finds a very high-fidelity factorization. The paper's experiments show 1-2% accuracy drop at 24-30% compression, which is much better than earlier compression methods because the shared-basis structure better matches how experts actually behave.

Additionally, the paper finds that the factorization is even more accurate when basis matrices B are initialized with structure (using activation functions like SiLU or tanh, which are mathematical functions that add structure, or Z-score normalization) rather than random because a structured starting point gives the optimizer better hills and valleys to navigate down, avoiding poor local minima. This structure helps B capture the core patterns that most experts share because the structured initialization already encodes some of the common behavior experts need, so the optimizer has less distance to travel.

stages.s: decompose W into A and candidate B matrices
select shared B that minimizes reconstruction error across all experts
tune each expert A to fit its expert residual
compressed model: one B per layer plus all A matrices

math.words: The weight matrix W is factorized as the product of two smaller matrices: W equals A times B, where A is the expert-specific transformation (unique to expert i) and B is the shared basis matrix (shared across all experts in the MoE layer).
math.equation: W_i = A_i * B, where A_i is expert-specific and B is layer-wide shared
symbols: original weight matrix of expert i
small expert-specific transformation matrix for expert i
large shared basis matrix, same across all experts in the layer

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose expert 1 has an original weight matrix W_1 that is 32 by 32 (1024 values).
We factor it as A_1 times B where A_1 is 32 by 8 (256 values) and B is 8 by 32 (256 values).
Total storage for expert 1: 256 plus 256 equals 512 values, half the original 1024.
Now suppose there are 8 experts in the layer. Normally: 8 times 1024 equals 8192 values total.
With MoBE: (8 times 256 for all A matrices) plus (256 for the shared B) equals 2048 plus 256 equals 2304 values.
Compression ratio: 2304 divided by 8192 equals 28%, or a 72% reduction.

math.note: At inference the model computes input times A times B, which gives the same result as input times W, but uses far less stored memory. The subscripts are explained in the symbol table.

charts.title: Expert Pruning (Naive)
charts.note: Removing experts loses specialized knowledge. Accuracy drops 11-14 points because certain tasks lose their expert.

charts.title: SVD Decomposition (Prior Method)
charts.note: Treating each expert independently, standard matrix compression loses information. Accuracy drops 7-9 points.

charts.title: MoBE (Shared Basis Method)
charts.note: Exploiting shared structure, MoBE preserves 94-95% accuracy even at 24-30% compression because B captures the common patterns all experts rely on.

items.html: If the shared basis B has too few columns (too much compression), it cannot capture the variation across experts. Reconstruction error grows, and model accuracy drops. The paper finds that the number of basis matrices m must scale with expert diversity and layer size.

If B starts as random noise, gradient descent gets stuck in a local optimum and never finds a good shared pattern because the error function has many valleys, and random noise lands in a bad one. The paper shows that initializing with structured activation functions (SiLU or tanh) or Z-score normalization dramatically improves convergence and final accuracy because structure provides a better starting point that is already partway toward capturing real expert patterns.

The paper tried alternating between updating A and B separately (an alternating optimization algorithm), but found it unstable during training because when you update A without B, and then B without A, the two chase each other and oscillate rather than converge. Adam optimizer (updating all parameters jointly) worked much better because all adjustments happen together, so A and B coordinate smoothly toward a single solution.

For extremely large layers (e.g., 384 experts in Kimi-K2-Instruct), jointly optimizing all experts at once is computationally expensive and can diverge. The paper solved this by splitting experts into sequential groups (two groups of 64 basis matrices each) and training them separately, which is a practical workaround but adds a tuning knob.

Choose the basis count m based on the target compression ratio and layer size. Initialize B with structure. Use Adam to optimize jointly. For huge layers, split into groups. Validate reconstruction error per layer before deployment.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny Mixture-of-Experts model (say, 4 experts, each a 64-by-64 weight matrix) and compress it with MoBE. Train the compressed model on a toy dataset (e.g., synthetic classification with 10 classes). Measure accuracy on a held-out test set before compression, after basic expert pruning, after SVD compression, and after MoBE. Separately plot the per-layer reconstruction error (MSE) for MoBE versus the competing methods. Show that MoBE achieves both lower reconstruction error and higher test accuracy at the same compression ratio.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy_drop equals (accuracy_before minus accuracy_after) divided by accuracy_before times 100%, reported as percentage; reconstruction_MSE equals mean of (W_i minus (A_i times B))^2 across all matrix entries
demo.closing: The demo must make unmissable: when many experts share a common blueprint, factorization preserves far more information than treating each expert independently. Storage shrinks 24-30% but accuracy holds at 1-2% drop.
